statement: A board with 3 rows and 7 columns has a counter on each of its 21 squares. At a signal, every counter moves one diagonal step, to a square that touches its own square only at a corner. Several counters may land on the same square. What is the smallest possible number of empty squares afterwards?

choices.misconception: I used the usual chessboard colouring, 11 squares of one colour and 10 of the other, as if every move changed colour, but a diagonal step keeps the same colour.
I coloured in vertical stripes: only the 9 counters in columns 2, 4 and 6 can reach the 12 squares in columns 1, 3, 5 and 7, so I stopped at 3, but horizontal stripes force more.
I thought every square in an odd row and an odd column stays empty, forgetting that the counters in row 2, columns 2, 4 and 6, move onto those squares.
I thought every square in rows 1 and 3 is left empty, forgetting that the 7 counters from row 2 move into those rows.

hints: Colour the board in stripes rather than like a chessboard.
Every diagonal step changes both the row and the column. Try stripes in both directions: which colouring forces more squares to stay empty? Then check that number can really happen.
Rows 1 and 3 have 14 squares, but only the 7 counters from row 2 can land there. Now find moves that leave exactly 7 empty.

solutions.reliable: Colour rows 1 and 3 grey (14 squares) and row 2 white (7 squares). A diagonal step always moves one row up or down, so it changes colour, and the grey squares can only receive the 7 counters that started in row 2. So at least $14 - 7 = 7$ grey squares are empty. Seven is possible. The counters in row 2, columns 1 to 6, move up and to the right, onto row 1, columns 2 to 7, and the counter in row 2, column 7, moves down and to the left, onto row 3, column 6: that fills seven different grey squares. The counters in row 1, columns 2 to 7, move down and to the left, onto row 2, columns 1 to 6, and the counter in row 3, column 6, moves up and to the right, onto row 2, column 7, so every white square is filled. The remaining counters move anywhere. Exactly 7 squares are empty. Vertical stripes only show that 3 squares must be empty, which is true but too weak. The transferable idea: choose the colouring so that every move changes colour and the two colours are as unequal as possible, then check the bound can be reached.

whyOnTest: Colouring arguments depend on picking the right colouring: the chessboard pattern says nothing about diagonal steps, and of the two stripe directions only one gives the answer.
